A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RBS research. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable matching despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original experiments on set generation, GridWorld, bit sequences, TF Bind, and AMP, including ablations and generalization tests in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds offline learning, downstream fine-tuning, RNA generation, and further comparison and robustness experiments.

M1.justification: The core RBS algorithm, loss, age-based sampling, backward regularization, reward intensification, and hierarchical decomposition remain unchanged. Appendix C.3 adds an offline adaptation using a fixed initial dataset instead of online forward collection, while retaining backward synthesis and Eq. (6). Appendix D.5 also reports an adaptation built on stochastic GFN.

E1.justification: v2 adds RNA generation, offline GridWorld learning without further environment interaction, downstream bit-sequence generation under unseen rewards, and stochastic GridWorld environments. These materially extend the evaluated domains and task conditions beyond v1's retained benchmarks.

E2.justification: Figure 1 replaces GFN+HER with OC-GAFN in the set-generation comparison. Appendix D adds an evaluated model-based GC-RL comparator combining ideas from MHER and DreamerV3, plus an RBS variant using prioritized experience replay. These are substantive comparison additions; SAC was already evaluated in v1.

E3.justification: New protocols include offline training from 8,016 trajectories on horizons 8, 16, and 32 (Figure 14), downstream evaluation using sphere-exclusion mode counts, stochastic transitions with random-action probability 0.01, and dense Manhattan-distance rewards. These supplement the retained online protocols rather than establish changes to their original settings.

E4.justification: Appendix D adds wall-clock efficiency analysis, sensitivity to the regularization decay coefficient, stochastic-dynamics and dense-reward robustness tests, and an age-based sampling versus PER comparison. The original backward-policy, reward-intensification, unseen-map, and SubTB analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report three random seeds with means and standard deviations. The added offline and stochastic experiments retain three-seed reporting; no new uncertainty-estimation method, significance test, or increased run count is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds near-100% offline RBS success rates, downstream mode-discovery results, RNA results, and outcomes for the new efficiency, robustness, and comparator experiments. Figure 1 replaces baseline result entries while retaining the RBS curve. Most original benchmark curves remain unchanged, so the additions are not same-setting performance improvements over v1.

T1.justification: Appendix A rewrites the gradient derivation into Eqs. (8)–(12). With Z defined as the log residual and the loss equal to Z squared, v2 writes the derivative using 2Z times the derivative of log Z, rather than Z. This introduces a localized mathematical inconsistency absent from v1's direct chain-rule expansion.

C1.justification: The central claims about backward synthesis improving sample efficiency and goal-reaching remain. v2 explicitly adds offline data-coverage challenges to the abstract and introduction, and replaces problem formulation in the headline contribution list with the already-existing training-stabilization techniques.

C2.justification: New Appendix E explicitly discusses reliance on known, structured dynamics and the limitations of discrete environments, leaving unknown dynamics and continuous settings for future work. Additional interpretations explain PER's poorer performance through persistent high losses and restricted data coverage, and discuss task-dependent reward scaling and performance reductions under stochastic dynamics.

D1.justification: v2 adds a project-code link, offline dataset construction and training instructions, and implementation information for the new comparisons, including PER parameters. The original architecture, optimizer settings, replay buffer, batch size, and hardware disclosures remain. Some release statements still describe code availability as future, so actual availability is not established by the PDFs.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against backward-model and model-based goal-conditioned RL in Appendix E.2, including Goyal, Hoftmann, and related work. It also adds Roy's goal-conditioned GFlowNet work and further GFlowNet–RL connections. This extends the discussion beyond v1's primary comparison with hindsight relabeling.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are substantially rewritten around data coverage, offline learning, and training stability. Problem formulation moves into preliminaries, the method precedes related work, and the supplementary material is reorganized into detailed experimental subsections and a new limitations appendix. Ethics and reproducibility statements are also added.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a different conference layout and resizes and repositions many existing figures. It adds Figures 5, 12, and 14–16 for new experiments, revises Figure 1's legend and vertical scale, and combines v1's separate SAC and TF Bind SubTB figures into Figure 17. The unseen-map displays are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: The wall-clock evaluation, downstream transfer study, and comparisons with model-based GC-RL and PER address important gaps in v1's evidence for efficiency and practical usefulness. New robustness tests and explicit applicability limits further strengthen the paper. These substantial empirical and interpretive gains outweigh the localized new chain-rule error in Appendix A, although the fine-tuning protocol remains incompletely specified.
